traveler: Atahualpa (Ataw Wallpa), last Sapa Inca of Tawantinsuyu
title: The Northern Court to the Plaza at Cajamarca: the War of the Two Brothers, the Room of Gold, and the Rope
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Cuzco, the birth the chroniclers give him
stops.date_confidence: contested on both counts. No contemporary birth record of any kind exists; the range c. 1497-1502 is a modern convention, and 1502 is used here only to order the segment. Cieza de Leon and several colonial testimonies favour Cuzco; a northern tradition claims Inca-Caranqui, carried as the next stop. Pinned at the Qorikancha because no source names a birth chamber.
stops.campa: A son is born to Huayna Capac, ruler of the four quarters, in the city where the sun is kept. Cuzco is the navel: four roads leave it for four directions, and at its heart the Qorikancha carries plates of beaten gold on its walls and the dried bodies of the dead kings seated in the dark, still served their meals at the proper hours. The men who will write this down are not born yet. No two of them will agree on the year, and half of them will not agree on the city. All of them give him the same father.
suggested_refs: The Qorikancha, Cuzco, in its pre-conquest state, gold plate and the seated mallquis of the dead Incas
sources: Cieza de Leon, via the dossier's synthesis of the colonial chronicle tradition

stops.name: Inca-Caranqui, the birth the north claims
stops.date_confidence: traditional and unresolved. Atahualpa is reported to have claimed this birthplace himself on the morning of his death. The fuller version, with the Shyri princess Paccha, comes from Juan de Velasco's Historia del Reino de Quito (1789), two and a half centuries after the fact, not read for this file. Coordinates approximate: the source gives Ibarra's centre and places Inca-Caranqui about 2 km off, with no point. The date only orders the segment against the Cuzco claim.
stops.campa: Two kilometres from where Ibarra will stand, in the Caranqui country that Huayna Capac took by war and then settled with his own people, a second tradition puts the birth. Quito tells it with a princess in it: Paccha, daughter of the beaten Shyri line, married to the man who beat it. Ecuador keeps this version and teaches it. Peru keeps the other. The cut stone at Caranqui is in the ground either way, and carries no date and no name. The claim is said to have come from Atahualpa's own mouth in the plaza at Cajamarca on the last morning, with the garrote already set up behind him.
suggested_refs: The Inca stonework and ceremonial pool at Inca-Caranqui, near Ibarra
Juan de Velasco, Historia del Reino de Quito (1789), carrier of the Paccha tradition

stops.name: Tomebamba, the second Cuzco
stops.date_confidence: inferred, and the date is an ordering device only. That Huayna Capac built Tomebamba into a northern capital is attested; that Atahualpa was raised in its court is inference from his later power base. No source names him at this site as a child. The research pool carried this at attested with a round date of 1520; both were corrected down for this file.
stops.campa: Huayna Capac builds at Tomebamba a city on the plan of the capital, with its own Qorikancha, its own house of chosen women, its own square laid out for the same festivals, and he keeps his court there for years at a stretch while the armies push north. Stone is dressed and carried from Cuzco itself so that the walls will be the right stone. A second capital is useful to a king who holds both of them. Huayna Capac holds both of them until 1525 or thereabouts, and then he is dead in the north and two of his sons are alive.
suggested_refs: The Pumapungo terraces and foundations at Cuenca, Ecuador, the surviving fabric of Tomebamba

stops.name: Quito, thirteen years old in his father's column
stops.date_confidence: later chronicle tradition, not independently datable. en.wikipedia gives the boy's participation in Huayna Capac's northern campaigns without a visible primary citation. The year orders the segment and is not a document.
stops.campa: The northern war goes on for years: the Pasto, the Caranqui, the Cayambe, all of them fought over ground that will not stay taken. The boy of about thirteen is said to march with his father in it, learning the country by walking it, learning the generals by name and by temper. Nothing in the record puts him in a fight, or gives him a command, or says how long he was out. Chalcuchimac and Quizquiz are in these columns. Rumiñahui is in these columns. Twenty years on, all three of them are still taking his orders.
suggested_refs: The Inca frontier works in the Otavalo and Cayambe country, ground of Huayna Capac's last campaigns

stops.name: Quito, the pestilence in the northern court
stops.date_confidence: unresolved three ways and not adjudicated here. en.wikipedia 'Huayna Capac' gives 1527 at Tumipampa; en.wikipedia 'Tumipampa' gives about 1525; en.wikipedia 'Atahualpa' gives around 1525. Place is disputed between Quito and Tomebamba; the Quito pin follows the northern-court tradition and is not a decision. The identification of the disease as smallpox is also disputed: the same Huayna Capac article records that his mummy showed no pockmarks.
stops.campa: A sickness comes down the roads ahead of any Spaniard, out of the Caribbean and through the isthmus and along the coast, and it reaches the northern court before anyone in Tawantinsuyu has seen a European face. Huayna Capac takes it and dies of it. Ninan Cuyuchi, the son he has named to follow him, dies of it in the same season. The empire loses its ruler and its designated heir inside a few weeks, to an agent nobody can name, sent by nobody anyone can march against. Whether the ground under the deathbed is Quito's or Tomebamba's, the sources cannot say.
suggested_refs: The Andean epidemic of the 1520s, arriving in advance of any European contact

stops.name: Cuzco, the fringe goes to Huascar
stops.date_confidence: attested that Huascar (Topa Cusi Huallpa) was installed as Sapa Inca at Cuzco after his father's death; the year follows the 1527 tradition and is soft in the same way the death date is. Pin inherited byte-identical from pizarro.journey.json.
stops.campa: In Cuzco the panacas and the priesthood raise up Topa Cusi Huallpa, called Huascar, and put on him the mascaipacha, the red fringe that no man wears twice. He is a son of Huayna Capac by a full sister of the royal line, born in the capital, crowned in the capital, seated among the dead kings who are carried out into the square for the great feasts and consulted. By the reckoning that Cuzco uses, that is the whole of the argument. There is another reckoning eight hundred leagues north, where the army is.
suggested_refs: The mascaipacha, the imperial fringe of the Sapa Inca, and the panaca corporations of Cuzco

stops.name: Quito, the north kept back
stops.date_confidence: reported, and the sources do not agree on the mechanism. Some say Atahualpa was made governor of the northern territory by his father's arrangement; others that he assumed the position. The file does not choose between them. Month and day default to order the segment.
stops.campa: Atahualpa does not go south. He stays with the veteran army in the country it has spent twenty years conquering, among the garrisons and the storehouses and the commanders who know him, and he holds the north. Some accounts make this his father's arrangement, a governorship left to him by design. Others make it a thing he takes and then calls a governorship. Both accounts describe the same map: two brothers, two capitals, one road system, and a chain of tambos down the spine of the Andes. Runners are on that road in both directions for the next two years.
suggested_refs: The Qhapaq Nan, the imperial road, and the tambo relay system linking Quito to Cuzco

stops.name: Tomebamba, the quarrel finds its shape
stops.date_confidence: the breach is attested; its cause is not. Cieza de Leon, Betanzos and Sarmiento de Gamboa each give a different precipitating incident: an embassy snubbed or killed, a suspicion of separatism, a straight rival claim. The file carries the disagreement instead of resolving it. Year is approximate.
stops.campa: What actually starts it is a question with three answers and no witness. One chronicler has an embassy from the north received badly in Cuzco and sent home shamed. Another has Huascar reading the northern army as a country in the making and moving first. A third has neither brother needing a pretext, because there is only one fringe. The Canari of Tomebamba, who have their own memory of being conquered, take Huascar's side. Which of the three is describing the actual quarrel, and which is describing what a chronicler's informants wanted remembered afterwards, nobody has established.
suggested_refs: The Canari of the Tomebamba basin and their alignment with Cuzco against the northern court
sources: Dossier synthesis of Cieza de Leon, Betanzos and Sarmiento de Gamboa

segments.name: The War of the Two Brothers

stops.name: Mocha, beaten at Chillopampa
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The en.wikipedia 'Atahualpa' battle list records Chillopampa as a defeat inflicted on Atahualpa by Huascar's forces; no primary account of the engagement was read. The coordinate is corrected from the research pool's -1.3654 / -78.6167, about 7.5 km off, to the figure en.wikipedia 'Mocha Canton' gives for the town, 1 25 S 78 40 W. Year approximate.
stops.campa: The war opens badly for the north. In the valley country below the volcanoes, at a place the chronicles call Chillopampa near Mocha, Huascar's army catches Atahualpa's in the open and breaks it. The road south closes again almost as soon as it was opened, and the northern army falls back onto the towns it came from. Nothing in the record says what the losses were, or who commanded, or where Atahualpa slept that night. The battle survives as one line in a list of battles, which is how most of this war survives.
suggested_refs: The en.wikipedia 'Atahualpa' battle list, the only surviving sequence for the civil war's northern engagements

stops.name: Tomebamba, taken and gone by morning
stops.date_confidence: tradition, preserved by later chroniclers and not by any eyewitness. The defeat at Tomebamba, the capture of Atahualpa, and his escape are reported together as a single dramatic episode; the escape in particular carries the marks of a story shaped after the outcome was known. Month and day order the segment.
stops.campa: Huascar's forces beat him again at Tomebamba, in the city his father built, and this time, the chroniclers say, they take him alive. He is held. He gets out. He comes back to his own army with the story already attached to him, and it is a story about a god rather than about a bribe. The versions differ on the mechanism: a woman brings him a copper bar and he digs through the wall; he turns into a snake and passes through it; someone is paid and nobody writes down who.
suggested_refs: The escape-from-Tomebamba tradition and its variants in the colonial chroniclers

stops.name: Ambato, General Atoc broken at Mullihambato
stops.date_confidence: date contested inside the research pool itself and not resolved. The geography lens gave c. 1530-1531; the en.wikipedia 'Atahualpa' battle list groups Mullihambato with Chimborazo and Quipaipan as April 1532 victories, which the file follows. Coordinates are the lens's own estimate for Ambato, unconfirmed by a fetched source. Whether Atahualpa was on the field or directing from behind it is not established.
stops.campa: The turn comes at Mullihambato, in the plain by Ambato, where Atahualpa's commanders meet Huascar's general Atoc and destroy him. From here the northern army stops defending the north and starts walking south, and it does not stop walking for a year. The generals do the fighting: Chalcuchimac, Quizquiz, men who learned the trade under Huayna Capac in the same campaigns Atahualpa learned it. Whether he is on the field at Mullihambato or a week behind it with the baggage, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: Atoc, Huascar's general in the northern campaign, and his defeat at Mullihambato

stops.name: Chimborazo, the second of the April victories
stops.date_confidence: date corrected. The research pool's chronology lens dated this 1529, conflating the battle with the war's opening year; the same site's geography lens and the en.wikipedia 'Atahualpa' battle list both give April 1532. The Chimborazo article itself carries no Inca-war content whatever; the connection rests solely on the battle list, which gives no detail of the engagement. Day within April is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Under the white cone of Chimborazo, on the paramo where the grass is stiff with cold and the air thins out, the northern army wins again. The list names three victories in this one month: Mullihambato, Chimborazo, Quipaipan, the last of them eight hundred leagues away at the far end of the road. Nothing else about this one was written down: not the day, not the commanders, not the size of either army. The chroniclers give the mountain because the mountain is the largest thing on that horizon.
suggested_refs: Chimborazo, the highest point of the Ecuadorian cordillera, named in the civil-war battle sequence

stops.name: Tomebamba, what is done to the Canari
stops.date_confidence: the reprisal is attested and the year is corrected. The research pool's chronology lens gave 1531; en.wikipedia 'Tumipampa' states the city was largely destroyed in the civil war before the Spanish arrival in 1532, and the geography lens agreed on 1532. Casualty figures are not recoverable from any source and none is claimed. Month orders the segment.
stops.campa: The north is recovered and the reckoning falls on Tomebamba, which held for Huascar. The city Huayna Capac built to be a second capital is broken up: walls thrown down, the population cut into, the Canari lords who chose the wrong brother made an example of at a scale the sources gesture at and never count. When Spaniards ride through the following year they find a ruin and are told what happened to it. The Canari remember too. They will remember it when the Spaniards need allies.
suggested_refs: The archaeological destruction horizon at Pumapungo, Cuenca, dated to the civil war
sources: Dossier synthesis of Cieza de Leon and later chroniclers

stops.name: Marcahuamachuco, the question sent to Catequil
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Coordinate corrected from the pool's -7.7975 / -78.1075, about 3.6 km off, to en.wikipedia 'Marcahuamachuco', 7 47 07 S 78 04 42 W. The Marcahuamachuco article does not mention Atahualpa; the connection rests on the en.wikipedia 'Atahualpa' note that while based there he sent an emissary to consult the oracle. The well-known tradition that he then destroyed the Catequil shrine appears in nothing fetched for this file and is not written into it. Month orders the segment.
stops.campa: Far south now, on the long ridge of Marcahuamachuco with its ring walls and its round towers built by people gone a thousand years, Atahualpa halts his advance and sends a man to ask a question. The oracle at Catequil speaks for the thunder and has been answering the Andes since before the Incas came. He wants to know what is going to happen. A year later, in a cell at Cajamarca, he will put the same kind of question to Pachacama and get an answer he can check against the outcome. What Catequil sent back this time is not in the record at all.
suggested_refs: The oracle of Catequil at Huamachuco, and the pre-Inca hilltop city of Marcahuamachuco

stops.name: Jauja, the storehouses of the other side
stops.date_confidence: attested that Xauxa served as the military headquarters of Huascar's faction, feeding and supplying his generals, and that Atahualpa's general Quizquiz took it. Atahualpa is not present. Pin inherited byte-identical from pizarro.journey.json rather than the research pool's rounder figure. Month approximate.
stops.campa: Xauxa in the Mantaro valley is where Huascar's war is run from: the storehouses, the levies, the grain and cloth and dried meat that keep an army in the field on a road with no wheels on it. Quizquiz takes it. The rows of round stone qollqas on the hillside above the valley pass from one brother's account to the other's in an afternoon, and with the depots gone the southern army is fighting off what it is already carrying. Atahualpa is a thousand kilometres north of this and hears about it within a few days, by relay runner.
suggested_refs: The Inca administrative and storehouse complex at Hatun Xauxa, Mantaro valley

stops.name: Quipaipan, the field he is not standing on
stops.date_confidence: attested, April 1532; the day is an ordering device. Coordinates approximate: the source gives only 'a couple of miles west of Cusco' with no point. Atahualpa was at Cajamarca, not on this field. The stop records an action carried out in his name and by his authority, not his bodily presence.
stops.campa: A couple of miles west of Cuzco, Chalcuchimac and Quizquiz meet Huascar's last army and destroy it, and take Huascar himself alive on the field. The war of the two brothers ends here, in April, in sight of the capital neither brother is standing in. No source gives the size of either army, or the day of the month, or what was done with the dead. Atahualpa learns of it a fortnight later, sitting in the north. By then his generals hold the capital, the treasury, the shrines and the royal mummies, and the crowned Sapa Inca is their prisoner.
suggested_refs: The field of Quipaipan, west of Cuzco, and the capture of Huascar

stops.name: Cuzco, Quizquiz in the capital
stops.date_confidence: attested that Quizquiz occupied Cuzco after Quipaipan and that Huascar's lineage and faction were purged. Numbers of the dead are not recoverable from any source and none is claimed. Atahualpa never entered Cuzco; the stop records the exercise of his authority there. Day orders the segment. Pin inherited byte-identical from pizarro.journey.json.
stops.campa: Quizquiz holds Cuzco for the absent king and goes through Huascar's house. Brothers, sisters, wives, children, the officials who served the losing brother, the panaca that raised him: the winning faction takes them out. The chroniclers describe it and do not number it. A panaca normally keeps its dead king's body, his household and his lands for as long as there is a Cuzco; Huascar's is taken apart while Huascar is still alive. Atahualpa is eight hundred leagues away in a hot-spring camp. He has won an empire he has not yet walked into, and he has not been crowned in it.
suggested_refs: The purge of Huascar's panaca in Cuzco, 1532, as reported by the colonial chroniclers

stops.name: Los Banos del Inca, the hot springs above the town
stops.date_confidence: attested that Atahualpa was camped at the thermal springs outside Cajamarca with a large army when Pizarro's column arrived. Coordinate corrected from the research pool's -7.1479 / -78.4636, about 1.7 km off, to es.wikipedia 'Distrito de Los Banos del Inca', 7 09 49 S 78 27 44 W, which puts the baths 6 km from the city. Day orders the segment.
stops.campa: Six kilometres out from Cajamarca the ground gives up hot water, and Atahualpa is encamped at it with an army the Spaniards will later put in the tens of thousands, waiting out the last of the war in the steam. Two channels feed the bath, one scalding from the source and one cold from the hill, mixed to whatever he wants. He is thirty or thereabouts, undefeated since Mullihambato, with his brother in chains and his generals in Cuzco. He has all the time in the world. The messengers coming up from the coast say there are about a hundred and sixty of them.
suggested_refs: The thermal springs at Los Banos del Inca, Cajamarca, and the Inca bath structure preserved there
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Distrito de Los Banos del Inca'

stops.name: Cajamarca, the two horsemen in the camp
stops.date_confidence: attested; the embassy of Hernando de Soto and Hernando Pizarro to Atahualpa's camp is described in Hernando Pizarro's own 1533 letter to the Audiencia of Santo Domingo. Pin inherited byte-identical from pizarro.journey.json.
stops.campa: Francisco Pizarro's column, something between a hundred and sixty-eight and a hundred and eighty men with a few dozen horses, walks into an empty Cajamarca and sends two riders up to the camp with an invitation. Hernando de Soto puts his horse through its paces close enough that its breath moves the fringe on Atahualpa's forehead, and some of the men behind the king flinch. Atahualpa does not move and does not stand. He accepts the invitation for the following day. Those who flinched, one account says, are dead before nightfall.
suggested_refs: Hernando Pizarro's letter to the Audiencia of Santo Domingo, 1533, the earliest account of the embassy
sources: Hernando Pizarro, letter to the Audiencia of Santo Domingo (1533)

stops.name: Cajamarca, the book that will not open
stops.date_confidence: attested as narration by an eyewitness, contested as event. Pedro Pizarro has Atahualpa ask for the closed breviary, fail to open it, and throw it down. The famous variant in which he holds it to his ear and says it does not speak could not be confirmed in any source fetched for this file, and pizarro.journey.json follows that variant; the divergence between the two files is deliberate and flagged. Patricia Seed argues the whole episode is a later literary construction; her article is paywalled and was not read.
stops.campa: The friar Vicente de Valverde comes out into the plaza ahead of the soldiers with a breviary in his hands and talks, through an interpreter, about a god and about a king in Spain. Atahualpa asks for the book. Valverde closes it and gives it to him. He turns it over, cannot find how it opens, and throws it on the ground. Pedro Pizarro, who is in the square, records that much and stops. The version in which he holds the book to his ear and remarks that it does not speak arrives later, and is in none of the eyewitness accounts, and has been argued to be a literary invention.
stops.quote: The padre carried in his hands a breviary from which he read the matters which he preached. Atabalipa asked him for it, and he [Valverde], closing it, handed it to him [Atabalipa]. When he had it in his hands he did not know how to open it, and he threw it upon the ground.
stops.quote_source: Pedro Pizarro, Relation of the Discovery and Conquest of the Kingdoms of Peru, trans. P. A. Means (New York: Cortes Society, 1921), vol. I, p. 182; eyewitness narration, brackets the translator's
suggested_refs: Patricia Seed, 'Failing to Marvel: Atahualpa's Encounter with the Word' (1991), on the episode as later construction
Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala, El primer nueva coronica y buen gobierno (c. 1615), Drawing 174, the seizure at Cajamarca
sources: Pedro Pizarro, Relation, trans. Means (1921), vol. I, p. 182
sites.utexas.edu/llilas-benson-magazine, 'Reading Between the Lines at Cajamarca'

stops.name: Cajamarca, the plaza at dusk
stops.date_confidence: the ambush is attested for 16 November 1532 by participant accounts; the day here is set to 17 only to order this stop after the breviary stop, which belongs to the same evening. Indigenous dead are reported by Spanish witnesses in the low thousands with no Spanish combat deaths; the totals are not verifiable and none is claimed. Pin inherited byte-identical from pizarro.journey.json.
stops.campa: He comes into the square on a litter of gold plate carried by lords in blue livery, with several thousand attendants who have been told this is a visit and are carrying nothing. The Spaniards are in the buildings around three sides of it. A gun fires, and the cry goes up, and the horse comes out of the doorways into a crowd that has no room to run, and the litter-bearers are cut down and replaced by other men who take the poles and are cut down in turn. Pizarro reaches him through the press and takes him by the arm. It is over inside an hour.
suggested_refs: The Plaza de Armas of Cajamarca and the surviving trapezoidal Inca fabric around it
sources: Hernando Pizarro, letter to the Audiencia of Santo Domingo (1533)
Dossier synthesis of Francisco de Xerez

segments.name: The Room and the Line on the Wall

stops.name: Cajamarca, the price he names
stops.date_confidence: attested by Hernando Pizarro's 1533 letter and by Pedro Pizarro. The room's dimensions are corrected: the research pool gave 17-18 feet by 35 feet, and no source contains any 35-foot dimension. Francisco de Xerez, via en.wikipedia 'Ransom Room' and es.wikipedia 'Atahualpa', gives 6.70 m long by 5.18 m wide with the line at 2.75 m. Whether the room was to be filled solid or with an agreed volume of objects is disputed and left disputed. Pin inherited byte-identical from pizarro.journey.json.
stops.campa: He has watched them for four days and has understood exactly one thing about them, and he offers it. The room he is held in, six metres and seventy by five metres and eighteen, filled with gold as high as he can reach standing, and the hall next door twice over with silver. He walks to the wall and puts his hand on it and they draw a line where the hand is, at two metres seventy-five. He sets the price himself, on a reading of these men he has had four days to make. Whether the room is to be packed solid or filled with an agreed count of objects is nowhere written down, and the two sides may never have meant the same thing by it.
stops.quote: Atabalipa said that he would fill with gold a room where the Marquis was, and that he would twice fill the big galpon, where, as I have said, the Spaniards collected together, with silver, as his ransom. In truth a great treasure!
stops.quote_source: Pedro Pizarro, Relation of the Discovery and Conquest of the Kingdoms of Peru, trans. P. A. Means (New York: Cortes Society, 1921), vol. I, p. 186; third-person report by the eyewitness, not a quotation of Atahualpa's own words
suggested_refs: The Cuarto del Rescate, Cajamarca, and the red line still marked on its wall
sources: Pedro Pizarro, Relation, trans. Means (1921), vol. I, p. 186
Hernando Pizarro, letter to the Audiencia of Santo Domingo (1533)

stops.name: Cajamarca, the oracle called a liar
stops.date_confidence: attested as reported by Pedro Pizarro, who was present at Cajamarca; the exchange is undated in the source and 1 January is an ordering device. The quotation is restored in full: the research pool had silently deleted the clause about the consultation over Huayna Capac's health, which is what makes the oracle's failure a failure, and had spliced two sentences into one. Page corrected from 213-214 to 209-210.
stops.campa: Pizarro asks him why he says the great oracle on the coast is no god, since his own people hold it to be one, and the captive king gives an accounting. Three questions were put to Pachacama and three answers came back, and all three were wrong: his father died, his brother lost, and the strangers won. He goes through them the way a ruler goes through a province's returns, item by item, and finds against the shrine. The third of the three failures is his own capture, and he counts it in with the others.
stops.quote: You should know, Lord, that when my father was sick [in] Quito, he sent to ask him [Pachacama] what should be done for his health. He [Pachacama] commanded that he be taken out into the sun, and when he was taken out, he died; Guascar, my brother, sent to ask him [Pachacama] who was to win the victory, he or I, and [Pachacama] said that he would, and I won it. When you came, I sent to ask him who was destined to conquer, you or I, and he sent to tell me that I was. You conquered. Therefore he is a liar, and is no God, for he lies.
stops.quote_source: Pedro Pizarro, Relation of the Discovery and Conquest of the Kingdoms of Peru, trans. P. A. Means (1921), vol. I, pp. 209-210; brackets the translator's
suggested_refs: The oracle of Pachacamac and the Inca practice of putting state questions to provincial huacas
sources: Pedro Pizarro, Relation, trans. Means (1921), vol. I, pp. 209-210

stops.name: Pachacamac, the shrine emptied under his safe-conduct
stops.date_confidence: attested that Hernando Pizarro's party travelled to Pachacamac in January 1533 and stripped the sanctuary, and that it went under Atahualpa's authority as well as Pizarro's. Atahualpa never went to Pachacamac; the stop records an order given from his cell and the safe-conduct that made the journey possible. Day approximate within January.
stops.campa: Hernando Pizarro rides for the coast in January with a small party and a piece of paper that is worth more than the party: the captive king's word, which still moves men on every road in the empire. The gold is prised off the walls and off the idol and carried back up to Cajamarca on the ransom account, under the authority of the man the shrine had answered wrongly three times. The priests got part of the treasure away before the party arrived and hid it. It has not been found since.
stops.quote: Atabalipa replied: Because he is a liar.
stops.quote_source: Pedro Pizarro, Relation, trans. Means (1921), vol. I, p. 209; his answer at Cajamarca when asked why he denied that Pachacama was a god
suggested_refs: The Painted Temple and the pyramid sanctuary at Pachacamac, stripped in 1533
sources: Dossier synthesis of Hernando Pizarro's letter and Francisco de Xerez

stops.name: Cajamarca, an empire run from one room
stops.date_confidence: attested as a general feature of the captivity rather than a dated event; February is an ordering device inside the November 1532 to July 1533 span. The exchange quoted is undated in Pedro Pizarro. Page corrected from 214 to 210.
stops.campa: For eight months the machinery keeps running through the wall of his cell. Runners come in and go out. Provincial lords arrive to be received and stand with their eyes down and a burden on their backs as they were taught, in front of a man under guard. Llama trains come up the road from Cuzco with plate stripped off the Qorikancha. He learns some Spanish, plays chess, has his food tasted, has every hair that falls from his head collected and burned. Nobody in the empire has yet decided to stop obeying him.
stops.quote: The Marquis said to him that he [Atabalipa] knew much. Atabalipa replied that [even] shopkeepers know much.
stops.quote_source: Pedro Pizarro, Relation, trans. Means (1921), vol. I, p. 210; brackets the translator's
suggested_refs: The chasqui relay system, still functioning under Spanish observation through the captivity
sources: Pedro Pizarro, Relation, trans. Means (1921), vol. I, p. 210

stops.name: Cajamarca, the room filled to the line
stops.date_confidence: attested. The gold reaches the marked line by late spring 1533 and the silver follows; the melting, assay and division are recorded in Pedro Sancho de la Hoz, Relacion para S.M. (1534), reached here through the dossier's synthesis rather than read directly. Pin inherited byte-identical from pizarro.journey.json.
stops.campa: It comes in as objects: vessels, ear-spools, plaques, seated figures, the sheathing off temple walls, a fountain, litters, the small gold maize that stood in the garden of the sun. The line on the wall is reached. Then the goldsmiths of Cuzco are put to work under guard melting all of it into bars, because bars can be weighed and split and a fountain cannot. Nine forges run for weeks. Every object anyone had made in that country for four hundred years goes through them and comes out the same shape.
suggested_refs: The Cajamarca ransom distribution record, and Pedro Sancho de la Hoz, Relacion para S.M. (1534)
sources: Dossier synthesis of Pedro Sancho de la Hoz, Relacion para S.M. (1534)

segments.name: The Brothers, the Generals, the Gold

stops.name: Jauja valley, Chalcuchimac called away from his army
stops.date_confidence: the research pool contradicted itself here and the file resolves toward the Jauja version. en.wikipedia 'Chalkuchimac' has Hernando Pizarro convincing the general, camped with an army of 35,000 in the Jauja valley, that Atahualpa had summoned him, and arresting him there. The rival tradition, that Atahualpa summoned him to Cajamarca and he was seized on arrival, is named here and not adopted. Month approximate. Pin inherited from pizarro.journey.json.
stops.campa: Chalcuchimac is sitting in the Mantaro valley with thirty-five thousand men, the largest intact force in the Andes and the one thing at Cajamarca that could be undone by a march. A Spaniard comes to him and says the king has sent for him. It is the one summons he cannot refuse and the one he cannot verify. He leaves the army where it stands and rides north to his lord with a small escort, and somewhere on that road the escort becomes a guard. The thirty-five thousand stay in the valley and are never used.
suggested_refs: Chalcuchimac, senior commander of the northern army, and the army left standing in the Mantaro valley
sources: Dossier synthesis of Pedro Pizarro's Relacion

stops.name: Cajamarca, the brothers who must not go up
stops.date_confidence: attested as reported by Pedro Pizarro, who was present; the episode is undated in the source and April is an ordering device. Page corrected from 196 to 192. Pedro Pizarro states that the brothers were killed on the road afterwards on Atahualpa's secret order; that attribution is the eyewitness's, made after the fact.
stops.campa: Some of Huascar's brothers are at Cajamarca and ask leave to go up to Cuzco, and the Marquis grants it. Atahualpa hears of the permission and goes to him about it. He does not say do not let them go. He says that if they go they will be killed up there, where they are not liked, and that when they are killed it will be said that he ordered it. They go anyway. Pedro Pizarro, setting it down as an old man about forty years afterwards, writes that they died on the road and that the order had been Atahualpa's.
stops.quote: Lord, give not this permission to these brothers of mine, for they are little liked up there [in Cuzco], and if they are killed, you will say that I ordered it.
stops.quote_source: Pedro Pizarro, Relation, trans. Means (1921), vol. I, p. 192; brackets the translator's
suggested_refs: The purge of Huascar's surviving brothers during Atahualpa's captivity
sources: Pedro Pizarro, Relation, trans. Means (1921), vol. I, p. 192

stops.name: Andamarca, the drowning of Huascar
stops.date_confidence: contradiction resolved and the resolution stated. es.wikipedia 'Huascar' gives June 1533 at Andamarca, also called Mollebamba, in the modern La Libertad region, on Atahualpa's order, the remains thrown in the river; en.wikipedia 'Jauja' independently has him held in a Xauxa fortress and later drowned in the nearby Andamarca river. The en.wikipedia 'Huascar' infobox value of 1532, Cusco is the outlier and is not followed. Coordinate is es.wikipedia 'Distrito de Mollebamba', 8 10 14 S 77 58 26 O, whose article states the death occurred in that district. A second Andamarca in Junin is a rival candidate, not adopted.
stops.campa: Huascar is being walked north under guard, toward Cajamarca, because the Spaniards have started asking about him and a spare king is a dangerous thing to leave alive in someone else's hands. At Andamarca in the Conchucos country the guards put him in the river. Most accounts say the order came from the cell at Cajamarca, and that the reason was precisely the interest the Spaniards had shown. The body goes downstream. Weeks later the killing of Huascar is read out as one of the charges against his brother.
stops.quote: That scoundrel Atabalipa, where is this gold and silver which he would give to the Christians? Does he not know that it is all mine? I myself shall give it to them, then they will kill him.
stops.quote_source: Pedro Pizarro, Relation, trans. Means (1921), vol. I, p. 189; Huascar's reported outburst on hearing of the ransom, prefaced in the source by 'they relate that he said', hearsay recorded by an eyewitness of other events
suggested_refs: The Andamarca river, Mollebamba district, Santiago de Chuco, La Libertad
sources: Pedro Pizarro, Relation, trans. Means (1921), vol. I, p. 189

stops.name: Cajamarca, the melting and the shares
stops.date_confidence: attested for June 1533; the day is an ordering device. The totals, roughly 1,326,539 pesos de oro and 51,610 marks of silver, come from Pedro Sancho de la Hoz's 1534 Relacion and the Cajamarca distribution record, reached through the dossier's synthesis and not read directly. Pin inherited byte-identical from pizarro.journey.json.
stops.campa: The bullion is assayed and cut up. The Crown's fifth goes off the top, then shares by rank: horsemen twice footmen, the captains more, Francisco Pizarro more again, and the sick left behind at San Miguel drawing something. It comes to something over a million and a quarter pesos of gold and fifty-one thousand marks of silver. Men who arrived in the Indies with nothing walk out of that square rich for life, and a number of them will spend the rest of it killing each other over the division.
suggested_refs: The Cajamarca distribution roll, listing every man of the company and his share
sources: Dossier synthesis of Pedro Sancho de la Hoz, Relacion para S.M. (1534)

stops.name: Cajamarca, Almagro's men, who own none of it
stops.date_confidence: reported. Diego de Almagro's arrival with reinforcements who had no part in the capture, and its effect on the incentives around Atahualpa's fate, comes through the dossier's synthesis of Francisco de Xerez and Pedro Pizarro rather than a single citable line. Day orders the segment. Pin inherited byte-identical from pizarro.journey.json.
stops.campa: Diego de Almagro comes up from the coast with a second body of Spaniards who were not in the plaza in November and are therefore not on the distribution roll. They watch the gold being weighed out to the men who were. The ransom has been paid in full. The prisoner who paid it is still in his room. From the day Almagro's column arrives there is a body of armed men in the camp that gains nothing from that arrangement continuing, and everything from whatever is taken next.
suggested_refs: Diego de Almagro's reinforcement column and its exclusion from the Cajamarca division
sources: Dossier synthesis of Francisco de Xerez and Pedro Pizarro's Relacion

stops.name: Cajamarca, the army that is coming
stops.date_confidence: reported. Rumours of an Indigenous relief force approaching Cajamarca in July 1533 come through the dossier's synthesis of Pedro Pizarro and other participant accounts. No such army was ever found. Day orders the segment.
stops.campa: A story starts in the camp that Rumiñahui is coming down from Quito with an army to take his king back, and it goes round a hundred and eighty men in a town of stone courtyards eight hundred leagues from any help. Sentries stand to all night. Horses are kept saddled. Nobody takes his clothes off to sleep. The army is never found, and no source ever locates it, and by the time it is clear that it does not exist the decision it forced has already been taken.
suggested_refs: Rumiñahui and the northern army at Quito, the force the Cajamarca rumour named
sources: Dossier synthesis of Pedro Pizarro's Relacion and other participant accounts

stops.name: Cajamarca, the two who would have spoken for him are gone
stops.date_confidence: reported. That Hernando Pizarro and Hernando de Soto were absent from Cajamarca when the final decision was taken is given by Pedro Pizarro and other participant accounts through the dossier's synthesis; the day is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Hernando Pizarro has gone to Spain with the Crown's fifth. Hernando de Soto is sent out on the road to look for the army that is coming, and rides for days, and finds quiet country. Those two had spent eight months in the room with him, one playing him at chess and the other taking his measure, and both of them thought the king was worth more alive than dead. The decision is taken while Soto is still out on the road. He gets back to Cajamarca after it has been carried out.
suggested_refs: Hernando de Soto's reconnaissance from Cajamarca, July 1533, and his reported anger on returning
sources: Dossier synthesis of Pedro Pizarro's Relacion and other participant accounts

stops.name: Cajamarca, the charges and the sentence of fire
stops.date_confidence: the proceeding is attested; its content is not. No complete authentic trial transcript survives, and the charge list, the procedure and any recorded vote reach us only through later and inconsistent retellings. The date is set the day before the execution to order the segment.
stops.campa: It is done in a room, quickly, with Pizarro and Almagro sitting as judges of a sovereign they have no jurisdiction over by any law either of them could name. The charges are read: that he usurped the fringe, that he killed his brother, that he killed his relatives, that he worships idols, that he keeps many wives, that he is raising an army against them. Some of these are true. The last one is the rumour that has been going round the camp for a fortnight. Not a single page of the proceeding survives in any authentic form. The sentence is burning.
stops.quote: Then Atabalipa wept, and he besought them not to kill him, for there was not an Indian in the land who would stir without his command, and he asked what had they to fear, holding him, as they did, a prisoner, and he said that if they were doing this thing for gold or silver, he would give them twice as much as had already been ordered.
stops.quote_source: Pedro Pizarro, Relation, trans. Means (1921), vol. I, p. 218; third-person narration by the eyewitness, not a quotation of Atahualpa's own words
suggested_refs: The reconstructed charge lists of the Cajamarca proceeding, preserved only in later chronicles
sources: Pedro Pizarro, Relation, trans. Means (1921), vol. I, p. 218
Dossier synthesis of colonial trial-charge lists

stops.name: Cajamarca, baptism, and the rope instead
stops.date_confidence: two traditions, both live, and the file follows the earlier date. Modern reconstruction gives 26 July 1533, on the ground that the expedition had already left Cajamarca by the older date; the older tradition gives 29 August 1533, the feast of the Beheading of John the Baptist, and sometimes the baptismal name Juan rather than Francisco. Both circulate in print. pizarro.journey.json uses 26 July and this file agrees with it. Pin inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: Valverde comes to him in the last hour with an offer. A man who dies a Christian is not burned, and a body that is not burned can be kept. Atahualpa asks whether they will burn him if he becomes a Christian, and is told they will not, and is baptized, and takes the name Francisco after the man who is killing him. Then they bring him out and set the collar on him and turn the screw, in the plaza where he was taken eight months before, in front of the same buildings.
stops.quote: And he asked if they would burn him should he become a Christian, and they told him no, and he said that if they would not burn him, he would be baptized, and so Fray Vicente baptized him, and they gave him the garrote.
stops.quote_source: Pedro Pizarro, Relation, trans. Means (1921), vol. I, p. 219
suggested_refs: Vicente de Valverde, Dominican, later first bishop of Cuzco
Peter Shaffer, The Royal Hunt of the Sun (Chichester, 1964; film, 1969), the modern dramatisation of this hour
sources: Pedro Pizarro, Relation, trans. Means (1921), vol. I, p. 219

stops.name: Cajamarca, the funeral and the fire in the clothes
stops.date_confidence: attested that a Christian funeral was held and that some of his clothing and hair or skin were burned to complete symbolically the sentence that had been commuted. The place of burial was never recorded and is unknown to history; no primary source confirms any later disposition. Pin is the Cajamarca coordinate guaman_poma_de_ayala.journey.json already uses.
stops.campa: They give him a Christian funeral with candles and a mass, and they burn his clothes, and some accounts say some of his hair and skin, so that the sentence of fire is carried out on a remainder. Then he is put in the ground somewhere in Cajamarca and no one writes down where. The two mestizo chroniclers who will make this hour known to Europe, Garcilaso de la Vega with his mother's Cuzco panaca behind him and Guaman Poma with his pen and his four hundred drawings, are neither of them born yet.
suggested_refs: El Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, Historia General del Peru (Cordoba, 1613), on the killing at Cajamarca
Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala, El primer nueva coronica y buen gobierno (c. 1615), Royal Danish Library, Copenhagen, digital facsimile 2001, ed. Rolena Adorno
sources: Royal Danish Library (kb.dk), 'Chronicle by Guaman Poma'

stops.name: Cajamarca, the fringe given to Tupac Huallpa
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Spaniards installed Tupac Huallpa, another son of Huayna Capac, as Sapa Inca at Cajamarca to legitimise the march on Cuzco, and that he was dead at Jauja within about three months. Day orders the segment. The stop is carried here as what became of Atahualpa's title, not as Tupac Huallpa's own journey; the operator may judge it a step too far forward and cut it. Pin inherited byte-identical from pizarro.journey.json.
stops.campa: Within weeks the Spaniards take a third son of Huayna Capac out of the household at Cajamarca and put the fringe on him, because an army marching on Cuzco does better with an Inca in front of it than without one. The fringe is put on him in the town where his brother was strangled a few weeks earlier, and the column moves off south with him at the head of it. Tupac Huallpa is Sapa Inca for about three months and dies at Jauja on the road south. The fringe goes next to Manco, another son of Huayna Capac, put on him near Cuzco in November of the same year.
suggested_refs: Tupac Huallpa, installed at Cajamarca, dead at Jauja in October 1533

stops.name: Malqui-Machay, the resting place of the mummy
stops.date_confidence: hypothesis, not established, and the file carries it as such. The Ecuadorian historian Tamara Estupinan proposes that Rumiñahui carried Atahualpa's body north and that this site, whose name means resting place of the mummy, is his last dwelling. The site has not been formally excavated and Estupinan's original publications were not located. Location corrected from the research pool's 'near Sigsig, Azuay', which conflated Sigchos with Sigsig, two places about 260 km apart; es.wikipedia 'Atahualpa' places Malqui-Machay in Cotopaxi province, canton Sigchos. The 1534 date orders the segment against the tradition of a removal soon after the burial; it is not a documented date.
stops.campa: In the Cotopaxi country, in the canton of Sigchos, there are stone walls and trapezoidal underground water channels at a place called Malqui-Machay, which in Quechua means the resting place of the mummy. A tradition says that Rumiñahui, who never surrendered, dug the body up at Cajamarca and carried it north to the country the northern version says he was born in, and hid it. An Ecuadorian historian has argued the case for the site and asked for it to be excavated properly. It has not been. The walls are still there and the ground under them has not been opened.
suggested_refs: Tamara Estupinan's identification of Malqui-Machay, canton Sigchos, Cotopaxi, as the last resting place of Atahualpa

stops.name: Cajamarca, the room that is still standing
stops.date_confidence: the structure and its identification with the ransom are attested; the date is an ordering device only, since no heritage-designation date could be verified. It is set at 1950 so that this stop precedes the Inkarri and stadium stops without breaking the segment's chronological order; it carries no evidential weight whatever. The World Monuments Fund's own page returned no retrievable content on fetch, so the description rests on en.wikipedia 'Ransom Room'. Coordinate corrected from the research pool's -7.1637 / -78.5128, about 800 m off.
stops.campa: One building of Inca Cajamarca is left. It is a stone room a little under seven metres by a little over five, with a trapezoidal doorway and niches in the walls, and a red line painted round the inside at the height a man can reach with his arm up. Whether it is the room itself or the room next door to the room has been argued over for a century and is not settled. Nobody argues about the line. It stands in the middle of a working town, behind a ticket office, off a street of shops.
suggested_refs: The Cuarto del Rescate, Cajamarca, the last standing Inca structure in the city

stops.name: Lima, the head beneath the palace
stops.date_confidence: oral tradition with no single origin date, documented by twentieth-century ethnographers among Quechua speakers, with variants recorded as far south as Huilliche and Mapuche communities in Chile. The 1955 date is purely an ordering device. The en.wikipedia 'Inkarri' article itself flags thin sourcing and names no ethnographer and no first documentation, so the myth's existence is attested while its documentation history is a gap. The identification of the Inkarri figure with Atahualpa specifically, rather than with Tupac Amaru I, varies by version.
stops.campa: The story that gets told in the sierra afterwards is that the body was cut up and distributed so that it could never be put back together, and that this failed. The head is under the government palace in Lima. The arms are under the square at Cuzco. The legs are in Ayacucho. Underground and out of sight the parts are growing back toward each other, slowly, at the speed of stone, and when the body is whole the head will come up through the floor of the palace and the world will be turned right side up again. Nobody says when.
suggested_refs: The Inkarri cycle in twentieth-century Andean ethnography, and its Huilliche and Mapuche variants

stops.name: Quito, the name on the stadium
stops.date_confidence: attested. The stadium was inaugurated 25 November 1951 as the Estadio Olimpico Municipal de El Batan and renamed Atahualpa in 1963; month and day of the renaming default to order the segment. Related monuments exist that are not staged here because he never went to them: the Atawallpa statue on the facade of the Palacio Real in Madrid, beside Moctezuma II, is the sculptors' work and belongs to Madrid.
stops.campa: The largest ground in Quito is opened in 1951 with a municipal name and renamed twelve years later for the man the city says was born two hundred kilometres up the road at Caranqui. Forty thousand people go into it on a Sunday. Peru has the plaza where he died and the room with the line still painted in it. Ecuador has the birthplace it claims and the hillside where the mummy is supposed to lie. Both countries teach him as their own, and neither of them can say where he is buried.
suggested_refs: The Atawallpa statue on the facade of the Palacio Real, Madrid, set beside Moctezuma II among the kingdoms of the crown
Painted portraits of Atahualpa at the Museo Nacional del Ecuador, the Ethnological Museum Berlin, and the Brooklyn Museum, all posthumous
